raw_response:
Start with **[Marginalia Search](https://marginalia-search.com/)** and **[Wiby](https://wiby.me/)**. They are particularly close to what you describe: ways to discover personally motivated pages that tend to disappear among larger commercial sites. Then try a personal-homepage community if you want the feeling of wandering from one person's interests into another's.

### Where I would start

1. **Marginalia Search.** Its own homepage says that it prioritizes non-commercial content and provides tools for both searching and discovering old websites. Try a subject that genuinely interests you, then explore beyond the first result. This is my strongest starting point when you have a topic in mind. Its preference for this material is not a guarantee about every result. [Official source](https://marginalia-search.com/). genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn302063197view0"}}

2. **Wiby.** Its stated purpose is unusually close to your description: finding pages made by hobbyists and other individuals about subjects they care about. The homepage also has a **“surprise me”** link, which gives you a concrete starting point for aimless browsing. I would try that when you want discovery rather than an answer to a specific question. [About Wiby](https://wiby.me/about/). genui{"citation":{"refs":["turn302063197view1","turn408217180view3"]}}

3. **Neocities.** Follow **Explore sites** from its [about page](https://neocities.org/about). This is a place for handmade personal websites; the project's own examples include fan shrines, digital gardens, project notes and online zines. Those are promising directions if the attraction is seeing someone's personality and interests expressed through an entire website. Individual pages will vary in substance, so treat the directory as a place to explore. genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn302063197view2"}}

4. **[MelonLand Surf Club](https://melonland.net/surf-club).** This is a webring and browsable collection of community members' homepages, with a random-site control. The current community rules focus on creative personal homepages and exclude commercial sites. A useful practical detail: if a member's page does not work inside the navigator, the wiki explains how to open it directly. Its current rules page was revised on **7 August 2026**, after your question date, so I cannot treat those exact rules as evidence of how it operated on 4 April 2026. [Community documentation](https://wiki.melonland.net/surf_club). genui{"citation":{"refs":["turn389106544view1","turn426067826view0"]}}

5. **[Search My Site](https://searchmysite.net/).** The operator's July 2025 report describes narrowing the index specifically to personal websites. That makes it another sensible place to search for a niche interest. The same report mentions paid listings, so I would describe its focus as personal sites rather than promise that everything involved is non-commercial. I verified the operator's report, not the live search endpoint. [First-party report](https://blog.searchmysite.net/posts/five-year-anniversary/). genui{"citation":{"ref":"turn587590285view1"}}

6. **[Kagi Small Web](https://kagi.com/smallweb).** Try this if you want currently active personal writing. Its launch announcement describes a curated route to recent non-commercial blog posts, and its public repository documents the project and feed access. The current inclusion rules are English-focused and apply restrictions to advertising and blog authorship; those rules should not be assumed identical to the launch criteria. This is a discovery route to personal content provided by Kagi, and I have not exercised the browsing interface itself. [Announcement](https://blog.kagi.com/small-web) · [Project documentation](https://github.com/kagisearch/smallweb). genui{"citation":{"refs":["turn408217180view2","turn408217180view0"]}}

**One additional lead to check:** [ooh.directory](https://ooh.directory/). It appeared as a blog-directory lead during discovery, but both its homepage and about page returned 403 errors to my retrieval tool. I could not verify its current first-party description or browse it, so I would keep it behind the documented options above. This is a verification gap, not evidence that the site is unavailable to an ordinary visitor.

For a first session, I would use Wiby's random link, search one of your book's subjects in Marginalia, and then spend time with a few homepages from Neocities or the Surf Club. When a page resonates, follow its own links and explore its older writing. That last step is my suggested browsing approach: the aim is to find an individual whose curiosity overlaps with yours and let their connections guide the next visit.

These recommendations concern documented discovery routes. I have not audited every destination for depth or commercial activity. Most current primary pages are undated; where I found a dated source or a known later revision, I have distinguished it above.
